evidence.quote: [[Image:Goat kid444.jpg|thumb|right|A goat kid.]] From {{inh|en|enm|kide}}, from {{der|en|non|kið||young goat}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*kidją}}, {{m|gem-pro|*kittīną||goatling, kid}}, perhaps from {{der|en|ine-pro|*gʰaydn-}}, {{m|ine-pro|*ǵʰaydn-||goat}} or {{der|en|ine-pro|*gidʰ-||kid, goatling, little goat}}. Compare {{cog|sv|-}} and {{cog|da|kid}}, {{cog|de|Kitz}} and {{m|de|Kitze}}, {{cog|sq|kedh}} and {{m|sq|kec}}. The sense of {{m|en|child}} has been in use since the 1590s as [[slang]], and since the 1840s in informal use.<ref>{{R:Online Etymology Dictionary}}</ref><ref>{{R:Grose Vulgar Tongue|page=124|passage='''{{smallcaps|Kid}}''', a child.|nodot=1}}</ref>

"the young of a goat," from a Scandinavian source such as Old Norse kið "young goat,"… See origin and meaning of kid. from a Scandinavian source such as Old Norse kið "young goat," from Proto-Germanic *kidjom (source also of Old High German kizzi , German kitze , Danish and Swedish kid ), a word of uncertain origin.

proposed_usageNote: This surface form has other senses (3 English etymology sections, young goat). The usage curve may mix them.
